newsitem.title: FRANCE: Delors raps Germans on EU monetary union.
newsitem.headline: Delors raps Germans on EU monetary union.

text.p: Former European Commission chief Jacques Delors accused German leaders on Wednesday of reducing European economic and monetary union to the sole issue of deficit-cutting at the risk of stifling growth and employment.

In a "letter to a German friend" published by the weekly Le Nouvel Observateur, Delors said some German leaders derided France when Paris called for a European economic government to balance out the power of a future European central bank.

He recalled that the Maastricht treaty provides for European Union member states to coordinate their economic policies and adopt joint guidelines, but such discussion had so far been academic with Germany refusing any joint investment plan.

"The best proof is the very concept of a stability pact proposed by (German Finance Minister Theo) Waigel. It is limited to controlling public deficits and punishing those countries which do not respect the criteria," Delors said.
"That is necessary but not sufficient to convince people like me who have constantly contributed to the construction of a strong, prosperous and fair Europe," he said.

"We have to draft a pact for stability and growth that will restore confidence between member states, give credibility back to the European ideal and allow us to make economic and monetary union a success for the benefit of our citizens," he added.
Failure to harmonise EU policies for investment and growth had cost member states an estimated four percentage points in gross domestic product since 1992, Delors wrote.
"That is why I disagree with German friends who reject the argument that our economies have paid a high price for an undervalued dollar," he said.

"It is not enough to reply with disdain, as they do, that this view shows a failure to understand the laws of economics and is motivated by a determination to combat the independence of the central bank," he said.
While exchange rates were set by foreign exchange markets, there were no grounds for resignation.
"It must be possible to influence the markets with an apprpriate monetary policy," he said.
However Delors criticised former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing who last week advocated an effective devaluation of the franc to boost growth and cut unemployment.

In a parallel "letter to a French friend", Delors said the franc was not overvalued against the mark and Giscard d'Estaing had given the Germans a pretext "to denounce a return of French laxness and brandish their diktat of 3.00 percent without taking into account either the treaty or economic reality."
